About Map Services

  • The Tiles Service value must be exactly openstreetmap or custom (a self-hosted tile server; set the Custom Map Tiles URL to a template like https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.png). Any other value, including "google" or "apple", silently falls back to openstreetmap -- there is no Google Maps or Apple Maps tile integration today.
  • The Geocoder Service value must be exactly nominatim; any other value (including blank) turns off automatic address-to-coordinate lookups.
Nominatim Usage

Nominatim's usage policy caps this at 1 request per second, which this app enforces itself. If deployed with multiple app instances, keep in mind each instance enforces that limit independently -- so N instances can collectively send up to N requests per second.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
What this page shows

These reports come from two separate, independently-recorded systems that don't share a denominator -- don't try to reconcile their totals against each other.

Top Search Terms counts page views that included a search query, logged once per page render regardless of what (if anything) was found.

Zero-Result and Trending search terms count actual search executions across six content types (pages, content, blog, wiki, items, calendar), each with its own real result count. A single visitor search can produce multiple rows here -- one per content type searched.

The reports further down break those same search executions down by content type, originating page, and near-miss (low-but-nonzero) result counts, to help narrow down where to focus. Like the tiles above, these are a floor, not a full census -- searches from logged-in staff and DNT/GPC-opted-out visitors aren't recorded at all.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
Content Analytics

Traffic and engagement across the site, grouped below by what each group of tiles is actually trying to answer. Every number on this page already excludes known bots and crawlers -- search engine crawlers, SEO/AI crawlers, and social-media link-preview bots, identified by user agent against an admin-editable list, are filtered out before these are calculated, so you don't need to mentally discount them.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
Traffic

How much traffic, and to which pages. Top Pages and Top Modules sound like the same thing but count differently: Top Pages counts every hit to a raw URL path (minus admin/login/asset paths), whether or not that path is a CMS-registered page; Top Modules only counts hits tied to an actual registered "Web Page" record, with no path filtering of its own. A path that's never been turned into a CMS page can show up in Top Pages but never in Top Modules, and vice versa for a registered page whose path would otherwise have been filtered out. Web Page Hits is a 30-day daily trend and, unlike the other tiles here, its window can't be changed from this page -- only Top Pages' own dropdown lets you pick a different range.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
Where Visitors Come From

Referrals lists the site that sent someone here (the HTTP Referer header), over the last 30 days. Two things it doesn't show: a visitor with no referrer at all -- bookmarks, typed-in URLs, some mobile apps that strip the header -- isn't bucketed as "Direct," they're simply left out of this list entirely; and visits from this site back to itself are filtered out as self-referrals, but only when the site's own URL is correctly set in Site Properties -- if it isn't, internal referrals could show up here as if they were external traffic.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
Engagement

What visitors do once they're here, all over a 30-day window. Return Visitor Rate is the trickiest of the three to read correctly: "active" is bounded to the last 30 days (has this visitor had at least one session recently), but "returning" checks that same visitor's entire history, not just the last 30 days -- so someone whose only prior visit was months ago still counts as a returning visitor the moment they come back, even though the actual return happened outside this window. A flat 0% here means either genuinely no return visitors, or -- rarely -- that the underlying query failed; the two aren't distinguishable from this tile alone.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
About Useful Links

These two lists fill in the two link columns shown in the footer of every public page on the site — the left column (Company) and the right column (Support), as labeled in the site footer.

Each row needs a Name (the text visitors click) and a Link. A Link can be an internal path (e.g. /contact) or a full external URL (e.g. https://example.com) — both are supported.

To remove an entry, clear its Name field and save; a row left with no Name is dropped from the list.

Looking for the floating action buttons shown on every page instead? See Sticky Page Buttons.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
About Sticky Page Buttons

This list controls a small floating button bar shown in the bottom-right corner of every public page on the site (it does not appear on admin pages). Unlike Useful Links, these buttons are hard to miss — changes here are visible immediately and prominently on every page, so double-check each link before saving.

A button automatically hides itself on the exact page it links to, so visitors are never shown a button that just takes them to the page they're already on.

Looking for a calmer, footer-column option instead? See Useful Links.

widget.title: Example
widget.html:
http -a username:password POST http://localhost:8080/api/oauth2/authorize X-API-Key:<secret_key>

This is a real human user login exchange (a username and password), not a machine-only credential flow. The X-API-Key header is the Client ID shown when editing an App on the Apps page -- it identifies which App is calling, but it isn't a secret.


{
  "access_token": "you-receive-this",
  "expires_in": 2592000,
  "first_name": "First", "last_name": "Last", "name": "First Last",
  "scope": "create", "token_type": "bearer"
}

The "scope": "create" value above is a fixed literal returned on every token response -- it isn't currently configurable and nothing in the platform enforces it. The access token grants the full access of whatever role the authenticating user already has, not a narrower scope.


http -A bearer -a <access_token> GET http://localhost:8080/api/me X-API-Key:<secret_key>

http GET http://localhost:8080/api/collections?key=<secret_key>

The APIs table below is a partial reference: it's generated by scanning this app's REST route configuration. oauth2/authorize is handled directly by the security filter rather than the scanned configuration, so it's added as a built-in row ("RestRequestFilter (built-in)") rather than a scanned one -- it does appear below, just not sourced the same way as the rest of the table.

widget.name: content
widget.title: About Apps
widget.html:
An App is a credential record that lets outside software authenticate to this SimIS instance's own REST API (inbound access). It has nothing to do with this CMS's own outbound connections to other services, such as payment processors -- those are configured elsewhere.

The Client ID shown when editing an App is not a secret -- it's safe to embed in scripts or share with a vendor. It identifies the caller but doesn't authenticate it on its own; an actual user login via the flow documented on the APIs page is still required for anything beyond public/guest-level data.

If a credential leaks or is otherwise compromised, use the Enabled toggle to disable the App immediately, then use Delete once you've confirmed nothing else still needs its history.

There's no per-owner filtering on this list -- anyone with access to this page can see every App in the system, and now that access is limited to admins. Periodically review the list for Apps you don't recognize.

widget.name: content
widget.html:
About MFA Enforcement

Roles that must enrol MFA: enter a comma-separated list of role codes (e.g. admin) whose members must have two-factor authentication enrolled before accessing any page. Role codes are matched case-sensitively. Leave blank to disable enforcement — no user is affected until a role is listed.

MFA enrolment page: the URL users are redirected to for MFA setup. This page must be reachable without MFA; the default /my-profile contains the two-factor authentication settings widget. This field isn't checked to confirm the page actually exists, so a typo here can lock everyone out — see recovery options below.

Saving requires re-authentication: because this is a security-sensitive page, Save will first ask for your password or authenticator code again if you haven't verified recently, then re-apply your changes once confirmed.

Before enabling: make sure at least one admin account already has MFA enrolled, and that the enrolment page URL is correct. Nothing enforces this automatically — enabling enforcement for the admin role while no admin has MFA enrolled will redirect every admin to the enrolment page on their next request.

Recovery, if someone is locked out: a locked-out user can self-service with one of their MFA recovery codes (issued at enrolment). If those are lost too, another sufficiently-privileged admin can use the "Reset MFA" action on that user's page under Users, which clears their TOTP secret and recovery codes. If the enrolment page URL itself is broken and no admin can reach it, the only remaining route is a direct database update clearing the mfa.required.roles value.

Changing this setting is recorded in the Security Audit Log as a setting.update event — that record is the governance evidence for SSP IA-2(1). Filter the log by event type setting.update and target type site_property to isolate MFA policy changes from every other settings page's saves.
